body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students describe how the shift from farm to factory changed work, family and wages, distinguishing the early textile mills from post-Civil War heavy industry (D2.His.1.9-12).
- Students analyze how a worker's circumstances shaped her perspective on mill work, and how a source's maker and purpose limit its usefulness (D2.His.4.9-12, D2.His.11.9-12).
- Students compare how an industrialist and a farmers' party viewed the concentration of wealth, and explain the government's first response to trusts (RH.9-10.6, D2.Eco.4.9-12).
- Students write an argument on industrialization's effects on workers that integrates evidence from several sources (D2.His.14.9-12, D2.His.16.9-12, WHST.9-10.1).

MATERIALS
- Readings in the activities: From Farm to Factory (background), A Mill Worker Writes Home, Carnegie's "Wealth," the Omaha Platform, the Sherman Antitrust Act
- A four-column sourcing chart (Sourcing, Context, Claim, Corroboration) on paper or in a shared document; students keep it all semester
- Optional: a map of New England rivers and mill towns; a photograph of a power loom from a public museum collection
- Important: A Mill Worker Writes Home is NOT a historical document. It is an original composite letter written for EducateOS from the experiences Lowell workers described in their letters, in the Lowell Offering and in testimony on the ten-hour petitions. Tell students on Day 1. Use it as a model source for practicing the four questions, and use the corroboration step to point them to real sources: the Lowell Offering (1840-1845), Harriet Hanson Robinson's memoir Loom and Spindle (1898), the 1845 Massachusetts House committee report on hours of labor, and company boardinghouse rules.

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Voices from the Mills aloud. Introduce the four historian's questions with an everyday example (a review of a restaurant written by its owner). Begin the lesson activity, From Farm to Factory, in pairs. Explain that the letter in this unit is a composite model source and why historians still must ask the same questions of it.
Day 2: Finish From Farm to Factory and debrief questions 4 and 5. Read A Mill Worker Writes Home together; students annotate for evidence of costs (red) and opportunities (green). Begin A Mill Worker Writes Home analysis.
Day 3: Writing workshop on the mill-letter analysis: model a sourcing paragraph that explains why Hannah might soften or sharpen her account. Students finish and submit. Exit ticket: name one real source that could corroborate Hannah.
Day 4: Gilded Age jigsaw: three groups read Carnegie, the Omaha Platform and the Sherman Act, then regroup to teach one another. Students begin Gospel of Wealth or Stolen Fruits?
Day 5: Unit assessment: Did Industrialization Expand Opportunity? (one class period, no AI help). Students may use their sourcing charts and the unit readings.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give a partially completed sourcing chart for the letter with the Who and When boxes filled in. Offer sentence starters: "Hannah may have written this because..." "This source is useful for... but limited because..."
- Support: chunk the Gilded Age readings: one short quotation, then the About the source paragraph, with a two-line summary box after each.
- Extension: students read a few pages of a real Lowell Offering issue or Robinson's Loom and Spindle (both public domain, available through public library and university digital collections) and explain how it confirms or complicates the composite letter.
- Extension: research the Homestead strike of 1892 and evaluate whether Carnegie lived by his own essay.
- Multilingual learners (ELL): pre-teach the key terms with a picture or gesture for each (loom, bell, wages, strike). Allow students to draft the claim in their home language first, then translate with a partner. Provide a glossary of nineteenth-century words in the letter: Sabbath, overseer, note at the bank, meeting, improvement circle.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit we are studying how factories changed American life between the 1820s and 1900, beginning with the young women who worked in the textile mills of Lowell, Massachusetts. Students are learning to read sources the way historians do: asking who made a source, why, and what it might leave out. Ask your student about the first job anyone in your family held, and whether it offered more freedom, more hardship, or both. Thank you for supporting our historians.
title: Teacher guide: Industrialization and Labor
